Simple guide

Delta Lake: Batch and Streaming

Short steps for notebooks 3.4c and 4.4c.

What you will learn
  • Write a Delta table.
  • Read it back two ways.
  • Go back to an old version.
  • See where data comes from (lineage).
  • Write with a stream and read at the same time.
Real values used below
3.4c tabledea_course.delta_batch.events
3.4c path/Volumes/dea_course/delta_batch/delta_files/events_delta
3.4c computeServerless
4.4c tableworkspace.default.events
4.4c checkpoint/Volumes/workspace/default/temp/checkpoints/events_stream/
4.4c computeClassic

1. Key words

  • Batch: runs once, then stops.
  • Stream: keeps running.
  • Micro-batch: one small batch in a stream.
  • Delta table: Parquet files plus a log.
  • Commit: one saved change in the log.
  • Checkpoint: where a stream saves its progress.
  • Volume: a governed folder in Unity Catalog.
  • Lineage: where data came from and where it went.
Notebook 3.4c

2. Set up

About this code
What
Creates a catalog, a schema, and a volume.
Why
Tables and files need a home.
When
First cell. Run once before anything else.
Where
Unity Catalog, in dea_course.
How, line by line
  • CATALOG, SCHEMA, VOLUME: names in one place.
  • DELTA_PATH: a folder inside the volume.
  • f"...": fills the names into the text.
  • CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS: create only if missing.
  • Safe to run again.
CATALOG = "dea_course"      # top level
SCHEMA  = "delta_batch"     # holds tables and volumes
VOLUME  = "delta_files"     # a folder for files

# Folder for the path read later
DELTA_PATH = f"/Volumes/{CATALOG}/{SCHEMA}/{VOLUME}/events_delta"

# Create each one if it is missing
spark.sql(f"CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS {CATALOG}")
spark.sql(f"CREATE SCHEMA  IF NOT EXISTS {CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}")
spark.sql(f"CREATE VOLUME  IF NOT EXISTS {CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.{VOLUME}")
Outputcatalog=dea_course schema=delta_batch volume path=/Volumes/dea_course/delta_batch/delta_files/events_delta
About this code
What
Sets the default catalog and schema. Drops the old table.
Why
So we can write events, not the full name. Clean start.
When
Right after setup.
Where
SQL cell (%sql).
How, line by line
  • %sql: run this cell as SQL.
  • USE CATALOG: pick the catalog.
  • USE SCHEMA: pick the schema.
  • DROP TABLE IF EXISTS: delete old table, no error if missing.
%sql
USE CATALOG dea_course;       -- default catalog
USE SCHEMA delta_batch;       -- default schema
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS events;  -- clean start

3. Write batch 1 (append)

About this code
What
Makes 10 rows and saves them as a Delta table.
Why
To create the first version of the table.
When
After setup.
Where
Table events. Creates version 0.
How, line by line
  • Row: one record with named fields.
  • random.seed(42): same values every run.
  • base_time: start time 09:00.
  • for i in range(1, 11): IDs 1 to 10.
  • createDataFrame: turn the list into a table in memory.
  • format("delta"): save as Delta.
  • mode("append"): add rows.
  • saveAsTable: save and register the table.
from pyspark.sql import Row                # one record
from datetime import datetime, timedelta  # for times
import random                             # for random values

random.seed(42)                            # same values every run
base_time = datetime(2024, 1, 15, 9, 0, 0) # start at 09:00

batch_1 = [
    Row(event_id=i,                                              # 1 to 10
        event_type=random.choice(["click", "view", "purchase"]),  # pick a type
        user_id=random.randint(100, 199),                         # user 100-199
        event_ts=base_time + timedelta(seconds=i * 30))           # every 30 s
    for i in range(1, 11)
]
df_batch_1 = spark.createDataFrame(batch_1)  # list -> DataFrame

df_batch_1.write \
    .format("delta") \
    .mode("append") \
    .saveAsTable("events")
# save as Delta, add rows, register table
OutputBatch 1 written — 10 rows appended.

4. Write batch 2 (overwrite)

About this code
What
Replaces all rows with 10 new rows.
Why
To show overwrite and create version 1.
When
After batch 1.
Where
Same table events.
How, line by line
  • df_batch_2: 10 new rows, IDs 11 to 20.
  • mode("overwrite"): replace all rows.
  • Old files stay on disk. Only marked removed.
df_batch_2.write \
    .format("delta") \
    .mode("overwrite") \
    .saveAsTable("events")
# replace all rows in one commit
OutputBatch 2 written — table overwritten with 10 new rows.
Overwrite is atomic
  • It happens in one commit.
  • Readers see old rows or new rows.
  • Never a mix.

5. Check history

About this code
What
Lists every commit on the table.
Why
To see what changed, who, and when.
When
After any write.
Where
The table log (_delta_log).
How, line by line
  • DESCRIBE HISTORY: show all commits.
  • Newest first.
  • One row per commit.
%sql
DESCRIBE HISTORY events;  -- one row per commit
Outputversion 1 06:04:28 CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE AS SELECT 10 rows version 0 06:04:25 CREATE TABLE AS SELECT 10 rows

6. Time Travel

About this code
What
Reads the table as it was at version 0.
Why
To get old data back.
When
Audits, fixing mistakes, old reports.
Where
Same table, older version.
How, line by line
  • VERSION AS OF 0: read version 0.
  • ORDER BY event_id: sort by ID.
%sql
SELECT * FROM events
VERSION AS OF 0       -- read version 0
ORDER BY event_id;    -- sort by ID
Output10 rows · event_id 1 to 10 · batch 1 is back
Limit
  • VACUUM deletes old files.
  • Default keeps 7 days.
  • After that, old versions are gone.

7. Read by path

About this code
What
Writes Delta files to a folder, then reads them by path.
Why
Some data lives in folders, not tables.
When
When data has no table name.
Where
The volume folder DELTA_PATH.
How, line by line
  • save(DELTA_PATH): write files only. No table.
  • read.format("delta"): read Delta files.
  • load(DELTA_PATH): from this folder.
  • count(): count the rows.
# write files only, no table
df_batch_2.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save(DELTA_PATH)

# read the files back by path
df_path = spark.read.format("delta").load(DELTA_PATH)
print(f"Row count: {df_path.count()}")  # count rows
OutputRow count: 10

Look inside the folder

About this code
What
Lists the files in the log folder.
Why
To see what a Delta table is on disk.
When
Any time you want to check.
Where
_delta_log/ inside the path.
How, line by line
  • dbutils.fs.ls: list files.
  • display: show as a table.
  • Each commit is one JSON file.
# list the log files: one JSON per commit
display(dbutils.fs.ls(DELTA_PATH + "/_delta_log/"))
Serverless tip
  • %fs does not work on serverless.
  • Use dbutils.fs.ls() instead.

8. Read by name

About this code
What
Reads the table by its name.
Why
Simple. Permissions and lineage apply.
When
Default choice. Use it most of the time.
Where
Unity Catalog table events.
How, line by line
  • spark.table("events"): read the table.
  • count(): count the rows.
df_catalog = spark.table("events")          # read by name
print(f"Row count: {df_catalog.count()}")   # count rows
OutputRow count: 10

9. Compare both reads

About this code
What
Checks that both reads have the same rows.
Why
To prove path and name give the same data.
When
After both reads.
Where
In memory. Nothing is saved.
How, line by line
  • exceptAll: rows in one, not in the other.
  • Check both ways and add.
  • assert: stop with error if not 0.
# rows in A not in B, plus rows in B not in A
diff = df_catalog.exceptAll(df_path).count() + df_path.exceptAll(df_catalog).count()
print("Catalog read vs path read — differing rows:", diff)

assert diff == 0, "reads differ"  # stop if not the same
print("✓ identical")
OutputCatalog read vs path read — differing rows: 0 ✓ identical
Managed tables
  • Read them by name.
  • Do not read them by path.

10. Lineage

  • Lineage is the family tree of your data.
  • It shows where data came from.
  • It shows where data went.

Simple example

  • raw_orders has raw data.
  • A notebook cleans it.
  • It saves clean_orders.
  • A dashboard reads clean_orders.
raw_orders  →  notebook  →  clean_orders  →  sales dashboard

Why it helps

  • Find errors: trace a wrong number to its source.
  • Before a change: see what will break.
  • Audits: prove where a number came from.

In Databricks

  • Unity Catalog records it for you.
  • No extra code needed.
  • Open a table in Catalog Explorer.
  • Click the Lineage tab.

In these notebooks

  • 3.4c: the notebook writes events.
  • 4.4c: the stream writes events.
  • Reading by name keeps lineage clear.
Notebook 4.4c

11. Clean start

About this code
What
Stops old streams. Deletes old table and checkpoint.
Why
A running stream keeps the cluster on. An old checkpoint can block new writes.
When
First cell of 4.4c.
Where
workspace.default and the temp volume.
How, line by line
  • spark.streams.active: list running streams.
  • q.stop(): stop each one.
  • CREATE VOLUME: folder for the checkpoint.
  • DROP TABLE: delete the old table.
  • dbutils.fs.rm(..., True): delete the old checkpoint folder.
for q in spark.streams.active:   # each running stream
    q.stop()                      # stop it

spark.sql("CREATE VOLUME IF NOT EXISTS workspace.default.temp")    # checkpoint folder
spark.sql("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS workspace.default.events")          # old table
dbutils.fs.rm("/Volumes/workspace/default/temp/checkpoints/events_stream/", True)  # old checkpoint
OutputClean start: table workspace.default.events and its checkpoint reset.
About this code
What
Sets the default catalog and schema.
Why
So events means workspace.default.events.
When
Before the stream starts.
Where
SQL cell.
How, line by line
  • USE CATALOG workspace: pick catalog.
  • USE SCHEMA default: pick schema.
%sql
USE CATALOG workspace;  -- default catalog
USE SCHEMA default;     -- default schema

12. Create the stream

About this code
What
Defines a stream of fake events.
Why
We need live data to test.
When
Before starting the write.
Where
In memory. Nothing runs yet.
How, line by line
  • readStream: read as a stream.
  • format("rate"): built-in test source.
  • rowsPerSecond 1: 1 row each second.
  • value: a number that goes up.
  • CASE: pick a type from the number.
  • 500 + value % 100: user 500 to 599.
  • current_timestamp(): time now.
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, current_timestamp, expr

stream_df = spark.readStream \
    .format("rate") \
    .option("rowsPerSecond", 1) \
    .load() \
    .select(
        col("value").cast("int").alias("event_id"),     # ID from the counter
        expr("CASE WHEN value % 3 = 0 THEN 'purchase' "
             "     WHEN value % 3 = 1 THEN 'click' "
             "     ELSE 'view' END").alias("event_type"),  # pick a type
        expr("cast(500 + (value % 100) as int)").alias("user_id"),  # user 500-599
        current_timestamp().alias("event_ts")           # time now
    )
# test source: 1 row per second

13. Start the stream

About this code
What
Starts writing the stream to the table.
Why
To have a live writer on the table.
When
After the stream is defined.
Where
Table events. Progress in the checkpoint.
How, line by line
  • writeStream: write as a stream.
  • format("delta"): write Delta.
  • outputMode("append"): add new rows only.
  • checkpointLocation: save progress.
  • processingTime="5 seconds": write every 5 s.
  • toTable: target table. Starts the stream.
query = stream_df.writeStream \
    .format("delta") \
    .outputMode("append") \
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/Volumes/workspace/default/temp/checkpoints/events_stream/") \
    .trigger(processingTime="5 seconds") \
    .toTable("events")
# Delta, add rows, save progress, every 5 s, into events
OutputStreaming query started. Writing to main.default.events every 5 seconds.
Note
  • The message says main.
  • It is only text.
  • The real table is workspace.default.events.

14. Read while the stream runs

About this code
What
Counts rows twice, 15 seconds apart.
Why
To show the read sees new stream rows.
When
While the stream is running.
Where
Same table events.
How, line by line
  • spark.table("events").count(): count now.
  • time.sleep(15): wait 15 s.
  • count_2 - count_1: new rows.
count_1 = spark.table("events").count()     # count now
print(f"Row count (read 1): {count_1}")

time.sleep(15)                              # wait 15 s

count_2 = spark.table("events").count()     # count again
print(f"Row count (read 2): {count_2}")
print(f"New rows landed by stream: {count_2 - count_1}")  # difference
OutputRow count (read 1): 105 Row count (read 2): 175 New rows landed by stream: 70
105Read 1
175Read 2
+70Rows added
What this shows
  • The stream and the batch read share one table.
  • The read sees new rows right away.
  • No copy is needed.

15. Stop the stream

About this code
What
Stops the stream and counts the final rows.
Why
A running stream keeps costing money.
When
When the demo is done.
Where
The running query.
How, line by line
  • query.stop(): stop the stream.
  • count(): final row count.
query.stop()                                         # stop the stream
print(f"Final row count: {spark.table('events').count()}")  # final count
OutputStream stopped. Final row count: 195

16. Check history

About this code
What
Lists all commits the stream made.
Why
To see one commit per micro-batch.
When
After the stream stops.
Where
The table log.
How, line by line
  • DESCRIBE HISTORY: show all commits.
%sql
DESCRIBE HISTORY events;  -- one commit per micro-batch
Outputv0 CREATE TABLE v1 to v38 37 × STREAMING UPDATE v29, v39 2 × OPTIMIZE (auto)
  • Auto OPTIMIZE merges small files.
  • v39 merged 33 files into 1.

17. Serverless vs classic

3.4c batchBoth
processingTime triggerClassic only
availableNow triggerBoth
%fsClassic only
dbutils.fsBoth

18. Recap

  • append adds rows.
  • overwrite replaces rows in one commit.
  • DESCRIBE HISTORY lists commits.
  • VERSION AS OF reads old data.
  • Read managed tables by name.
  • Lineage shows where data came from.
  • A stream writes one commit per micro-batch.
  • Batch reads see new stream rows.
  • Always stop streams.
Code and outputs are from the real 3.4c and 4.4c runs on 26 Sep 2026. Comments and animations added for learning.
